body.heading: Bigger words, more beats
paragraphs: You already know the trick: a syllable is a beat, and your chin drops once per beat. Now it is time for the heavyweight words — the ones with four, five, even six beats hiding inside.
Say each word slowly, chin on hand, and count the drops.

body.heading: Four-beat words
paragraphs: alligator — al-li-ga-tor (4). caterpillar — cat-er-pil-lar (4). watermelon — wa-ter-mel-on (4). helicopter — hel-i-cop-ter (4).

body.heading: Five-beat words
paragraphs: hippopotamus — hip-po-pot-a-mus (5). refrigerator — re-frig-er-a-tor (5). congratulations — con-grat-u-la-tions (5). university — u-ni-ver-si-ty (5).

body.heading: The champion
paragraphs: Can anything beat five? Try 'extraterrestrial' — ex-tra-ter-res-tri-al. Count the chin drops carefully… that is SIX beats, the champion of this chart.
Long words stop being scary when you read them beat by beat. That is the real secret of this chart: big words are just small beats holding hands.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Find the longest word in a book you are reading and count its syllables. Can it beat the champion?
2. Why do you think breaking a long word into beats makes it easier to read AND easier to spell?

takeaway: Even champion words surrender to the beat trick: hippopotamus has 5 syllables, and 'extraterrestrial' tops the chart with 6.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
safetyNotes: Reading only — no physical activity or materials are involved.
screenFreeExtension: After reading, close the screen and retell three things you learned to someone at home in your own words.
